questions.stem: Which planet in our Solar System has a sidereal rotation period (length of a day) that is longer than its own orbital period (year) around the Sun?

options.option_text: Mercury, the innermost and fastest-orbiting rocky planet
Venus, which rotates so slowly that its day exceeds its year
Mars, which has two small moons named Phobos and Deimos
Jupiter, which completes one full orbit in about 12 Earth years

questions.explanation: Venus takes ~243 Earth days to complete one rotation (sidereal day) but only ~225 Earth days to orbit the Sun — making its day longer than its year. Mercury is the most tempting distractor: its solar day (sunrise to sunrise) is 176 Earth days, which is longer than its year of 88 Earth days. However, Mercury's sidereal rotation (58.6 days) is shorter than its year; Venus is the standard example where even the sidereal day exceeds the year.

questions.stem: The large, dark, relatively flat regions visible on the Moon's near side, formed by ancient basaltic lava flows that solidified billions of years ago, are collectively called what?

options.option_text: Terrae, the bright cratered highlands covering most of the lunar surface
Maria, the dark basaltic plains covering about 16% of the Moon's surface
Rilles, the long narrow trenches caused by ancient tectonic stretching
Ejecta blankets, the debris fields radiating from large impact craters

questions.explanation: Lunar maria (singular: mare) are the dark plains formed when ancient volcanic eruptions flooded low-lying impact basins with basaltic lava. They cover ~16% of the lunar surface, mostly on the near side. Terrae (option A) are the bright, heavily cratered highlands that make up the remaining surface — early astronomers mistook maria for actual seas, hence the Latin name for 'seas'.

questions.stem: Jupiter-family comets — those with orbital periods under 20 years — are believed to originate primarily from which reservoir in the outer Solar System?

options.option_text: The Oort Cloud, a vast spherical shell extending up to 100,000 AU from the Sun
The Kuiper Belt, a disc of icy bodies extending from 30 to 50 AU beyond Neptune
The Asteroid Belt, the rocky debris band between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter
The heliopause boundary, where solar wind transitions into interstellar medium

questions.explanation: Jupiter-family comets (JFCs) are gravitationally scattered inward from the Kuiper Belt and its dynamically active extension, the Scattered Disc. The Oort Cloud (option A) is the source of long-period comets with orbital periods exceeding 200 years, such as comet Hale-Bopp. The distinction is testable in exams: short-period → Kuiper Belt; long-period → Oort Cloud.

questions.stem: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is stationed at which Sun–Earth Lagrange point, allowing its sunshield to simultaneously block thermal radiation from both the Sun and Earth?

options.option_text: L1, the equilibrium point located between the Sun and Earth at ~1.5 million km
L2, on Earth's anti-sunward side at about 1.5 million km from Earth
L4, the stable leading Trojan point located 60° ahead in Earth's orbital path
L3, the point diametrically opposite Earth on the far side of the Sun's orbit

questions.explanation: L2 sits on the far side of Earth from the Sun, allowing JWST's five-layer sunshield to block heat from both the Sun and Earth simultaneously — essential for its infrared instruments to operate at ~−233 °C. L1 (option A) is the location of solar-observing spacecraft like SOHO and ACE, as it has a continuous view of the Sun. Confusing L1 and L2 is the most common examiner trap here.

questions.stem: A sidereal day on Earth (23 hours 56 minutes) is about 4 minutes shorter than a mean solar day (24 hours). Which of the following correctly explains this difference?

options.option_text: Earth's axial tilt causes the Sun to shift slightly in its apparent daily arc
Earth's orbital motion means it must rotate slightly extra to face the Sun again
The Moon's gravity acts as a tidal brake, slowing rotation by about 4 minutes
Earth's spin speed varies seasonally, creating an average 4-minute discrepancy

questions.explanation: A sidereal day measures Earth's rotation relative to distant stars (~360°). A solar day measures rotation relative to the Sun. Since Earth moves ~1° along its orbit per day, it must rotate an additional ~1° (~4 minutes) to bring the Sun back to the same meridian — making the solar day longer. The Moon's tidal braking (option C) does lengthen the day over geological time, but by milliseconds per century, not 4 minutes per day.

questions.stem: The 'Grand Tack' hypothesis in planetary formation proposes a specific sequence of early Solar System events. Which of the following best describes its central claim?

options.option_text: Mars originally formed beyond 5 AU and was transported inward via Jupiter's mean-motion resonances
Jupiter migrated sunward to about 1.5 AU, then reversed outward as Saturn formed and entered resonance
Saturn formed first at 3 AU and spiralled outward on its own, gravitationally dragging Jupiter along
The proto-Sun ejected a super-Earth inward, ultimately triggering the Late Heavy Bombardment of the inner planets

questions.explanation: The Grand Tack hypothesis (Walsh et al., 2011) proposes Jupiter first migrated inward to ~1.5 AU via Type II disc migration, truncating the rocky-planet feeding zone and explaining Mars's small size. When Saturn formed and the two planets entered a 2:3 mean-motion resonance, the net disc torque reversed, tacking Jupiter outward to its current ~5.2 AU. Option A confuses the consequence (Mars's stunted growth) with the mechanism; option C reverses the sequence of formation and migration.

questions.stem: The Titius-Bode law predicts planetary distances from the Sun using a numerical series. For which planet, discovered after the law was formulated, does the rule most conspicuously fail?

options.option_text: Uranus, whose 1781 discovery at 19.2 AU closely confirmed the predicted 19.6 AU
Neptune, whose actual orbit at 30.1 AU falls far short of the predicted 38.8 AU
Saturn, whose orbit at 9.6 AU closely matches the law's predicted value of 10 AU
Mars, whose distance of 1.52 AU very nearly matches the law's predicted 1.6 AU value

questions.explanation: The Titius-Bode series (0.4 + 0.3×2ⁿ AU) predicted a planet at 38.8 AU for n=7; Neptune's actual distance is 30.1 AU — a ~23% shortfall that is far outside observational error. Uranus (option A) famously confirmed the law: predicted 19.6 AU, observed 19.2 AU, which is why Bode's rule was taken seriously enough to guide the search for a 'missing' planet at 2.8 AU (the asteroid belt, confirmed by Piazzi's discovery of Ceres in 1801). Saturn and Mars also fit the law well.
